lesson.title: Decimals to Thousandths: Tiny Numbers, Big Ideas

steps.say: Hi friend, it's Ms. Yuanyuan! Imagine you're holding a metre stick in class. You measure your pencil case and it isn't exactly one metre, and it isn't even exactly two tenths of a metre. It lands at two hundred thirty-five millimetres, which we write as zero point two three five metres. Whole numbers alone couldn't say that. That's exactly why decimals exist — to describe pieces that are smaller than one.

visual.caption: One metre split up small: the pencil case lands at 0.235 m

steps.say: Here's the whole secret, one small step at a time. Cut one whole into ten equal parts and each part is one tenth. Cut one tenth into ten again and each little piece is one hundredth — that's one tiny square in this grid of one hundred. Now cut that one tiny square into ten skinny slivers, and each sliver is one thousandth. Every time we cut into ten, we go one place further to the right.

visual.caption: The whole grid is 1. One shaded square is one hundredth — slice it into 10 to get one thousandth

steps.say: So each spot after the decimal point has its own job. The first spot is tenths, the second is hundredths, and the third is thousandths. Look at zero point three seven five. The three is three tenths, the seven is seven hundredths, and the five is five thousandths. Altogether that's three hundred seventy-five thousandths. We say it out loud as zero point three seven five, or three hundred seventy-five thousandths.

visual.caption: 0.375 — each digit sits in its own place

steps.say: Now here's the beautiful part, and it's this term's big idea. Seven tenths of the grid is shaded. You can call that seven tenths, or seventy hundredths, or seven hundred thousandths — the shaded amount never changed, only the size of the pieces we counted with. That's why zero point seven, zero point seven zero, and zero point seven zero zero are all the same number. Extra zeros on the end don't add anything.

visual.caption: 70 out of 100 squares shaded — the same as 7 out of 10

steps.say: Let's try one together. At the doctor's office your little cousin measures one metre and two hundred thirty-five millimetres tall. Since one millimetre is one thousandth of a metre, we write one point two three five metres. Read it like this: one whole metre, plus two tenths, plus three hundredths, plus five thousandths. We say it as one and two hundred thirty-five thousandths metres.

Here's a slightly trickier one. Which is bigger, zero point five or zero point four seven five? Lots of kids guess the second one because it has more digits, but longer doesn't mean bigger. Give them the same size pieces first: zero point five becomes zero point five zero zero. Now compare five hundred thousandths with four hundred seventy-five thousandths. Five hundred wins, so zero point five is bigger — by twenty-five thousandths.

visual.caption: 0.475 sits to the left of 0.5, so 0.5 is the larger number

steps.say: And that's it! Just remember the three little rooms after the dot — tenths, hundredths, thousandths — and when you need to compare, dress the numbers in matching zeros first. You've got this.

visual.caption: Can you read this one? Four hundred six thousandths!

lesson.answer: After the decimal point come tenths, hundredths, and thousandths — and adding zeros on the end (0.5 = 0.500) doesn't change the value, it just makes the pieces the same size for comparing.

practice.question: Maya's new pencil measures 0.125 m at the school store in Kelowna. First, how many millimetres long is it? Then, her friend's pencil is 0.13 m. Whose pencil is longer?
practice.answer: 0.125 m is 125 mm (since 1 mm = 0.001 m). To compare, write 0.13 as 0.130. Because 130 thousandths is more than 125 thousandths, the friend's 0.13 m pencil is longer — by 0.005 m, which is 5 mm.
